title: Chapter 105 – Lan Tong's Leaf
html:
[Red Ridge Manor – Lin Jian]

Red Ridge is not red. It is the color of old brick going to rust, a long low rampart of stone along the crest of a hill, with a manor house crouched behind it like a cat behind a wall.

Jian lies on his stomach in the frozen heather and studies it through the gap in a bramble. It is the evening of the fourth day of the eleventh month. The sun has gone down behind the western range, leaving a band of cold yellow along the horizon and a sky above it the green of old glass. There is no wind. Smoke rises straight from three chimneys. The great gate in the wall is shut, and above it a single lantern burns.

Beside him, flat on the ground, Zhao Bei breathes quietly and says nothing. She has her pick across her back and a coil of rope at her hip. She came out of the Gray Peak mine like a woman stepping out of a long illness, squinting at the sky, and for the first day she walked in silence, touching the trees. On the second she began to talk. On the third she talked about her mother's cooking. She has not stopped since, in low undertones, in a voice rusty with disuse, and he has found, to his surprise, that he does not mind.

"Eleven men on the wall," she murmurs. "Four I know. Two I trained. The others are new."

"Pei?"

"In the east gallery with his wine. It is the hour." She spits. "He always was a coward. When we were boys he cried when the dogs were put down."

"You grew up here."

"Until I was twenty-four. Then I went to the mines." She shifts the pick. "I thought it would be a punishment. It was a rest."

He says nothing. His left arm hangs in its sling, gray from shoulder to wrist, throbbing in time with the cold. He cannot lift it. He has a staff in his right hand, and a knife, and a ring of black iron wrapped in cloth against his chest. In his sleeve is Heng's deed. And in his belt, folded small, is the thing that has made this possible: a sheet of heavy white paper, stamped with the Outer Court's seal.

Court Writ, it reads. Enforcement Deputy Rong, acting under Article thirty-one, to take custody of the Red Ridge manor, lands, and persons, by the deed of Zhao Heng. The Gate Bearer, Lin Jian, to supervise.

Rong had sent it by a runner to the mine the day after Yan Zhi left. It came with one line, in her blunt hand: You are on a Court errand. You have been since the ninth. Do not make me a liar.

She has staked her badge, he thinks. As Qin Hao staked his name. The debt is mounting up in a ledger he has never opened, and one day someone will ask him to pay it.

"They come," says Bei.

* * *

Rong rides up the hill at the head of twelve Enforcement disciples, in silver and gray, with the Court's banner on a pole.

They come openly, by the road, at an easy walk. They do not hurry. The horses' hooves ring on the frozen ground, and the sound carries across the dusk like a drum. At the gate Rong reins in and lifts her voice.

"Open in the name of the Outer Court. A writ of custody, under the deed of Zhao Heng."

For a long moment nothing happens. Then a head appears over the wall, white-faced under a steel cap. "The master of the house is not at home."

"The master of the house is in the Law Pavilion's cells, dying. I know exactly where he is." Rong's voice does not rise. "Open the gate, or it will be opened."

Jian is already moving. He has risen from the heather with Bei at his shoulder, and they go along the rampart in the shadow, in a crouch, toward the north corner where a drainage culvert runs under the wall. Pebble has slipped from his collar and is trotting ahead in the dusk, snout down. Seam, it whispers. Here. Easy. Old. Its voice shakes a little. The pangolin has been walking the cold ground for four days, and has slept for none of them, and the seam-sense is a muscle that tires. He lays a hand on its back as it trots, and feels the small body trembling with effort.

The culvert is a hole as wide as a barrel, choked with frozen weeds. Bei sets her shoulder to the grating and heaves, and with a crack the rusted bars give way. They go in on hands and knees, through the ice and the dark, a stooping crawl of thirty paces, and come out under a yew in the manor's kitchen garden.

Voices. Boots. Behind them, over the wall, the crash of a gate being forced.

"East gallery," Bei says in his ear. "The back stair. Run."

* * *

The east wing of the Red Ridge manor is a long cold gallery of dark timber, with a row of narrow doors down one side and tall windows down the other. Lamps burn in brackets. The floor is polished. At the far end, a man in a fur-trimmed robe sits at a low table with a flask of wine at his elbow, his back to them, staring into a brazier.

"Pei," says Bei.

He does not turn. Then he does, all at once, upsetting the flask. It spills across the table in a dark bright stream. He is a small round man of forty with a soft white face and a wisp of mustache. A knotted red cord is wound three times around his left wrist. His mouth opens and shuts.

"Bei," he says. "Bei. You are in the mines."

"Not tonight."

"You cannot be here. The master said—"

"The master is dying, Pei. He has given me the house." She walks toward him down the gallery, with the pick in her hand, not hurrying. "I have come to take the boy."

"You can't." The steward scrambles backward from the table. His hand goes to his wrist. His fingers close on the red cord. "I'll— I'll do it, you know. If you come near. I'll pull. The boy will—"

"Do you remember when the dogs were put down?" says Bei.

Pei stops. His mouth trembles.

"You cried for three days. You hid in the hayloft." She is ten paces away. Eight. "I brought you bread. You said you would never hurt a living thing. You said it to me, on your knees, with straw in your hair." Her voice does not change. "What did they offer you, Pei?"

"A seat," whispers the steward. "A seat at the Treasury. Twenty years of work. A house in the town." His white face crumples. "I only had to wait."

"Hm."

She doesn't swing. She simply walks up to him and plucks the knotted cord from his wrist with two thick fingers, as one plucks a thread from a robe.

It does not break. Pei shrieks, and clutches his arm, and sinks to the floor in a heap, sobbing, and the cord lies in her hand like a dead snake.

"The knot is not on him," she says to Jian, without turning. "It is on the boy. This is only the end of it. Go."

* * *

The third door on the right is locked.

He stops before it with the iron ring in his hand. The lamp bracket beside it throws a trembling light over the dark wood. He can feel his heart going, a slow hard knock, and the weakness in his legs, and the cold in his arm. He can feel, in the other direction, a very small sound.

It is the sound of someone breathing, carefully, in the dark, to make as little noise as possible.

He fits the ring to the lock.

It is not a key, exactly. It is a loop of cold iron with a hook, and it slips into the keyhole like a finger into a glove. He turns it. A faint warmth comes up through the metal. Somewhere inside the door, a thread snaps with a sound too small to hear.

The door swings open.

The room is small and bare. A cot with a gray blanket. A window barred with iron. A bowl, empty, on the floor. And in the corner, against the wall, with his knees drawn up and his arms wrapped around them, a boy.

He is eight. He is thin as a rake. His hair is cropped close and his eyes are huge in a face the color of tallow, and he doesn't look up. He is looking at his own wrist, where a red mark circles the skin like a bracelet, fading as Jian watches.

"Hui," Jian says softly.

The boy doesn't move.

"My name is Lin Jian. I am a friend of your brother's. Yao sent me." He kneels, slowly, a few paces off, and puts down the knife and the staff. "I have a message from your cousin Qian. She says she is sorry. She says it was never your fault."

Nothing.

"Your brother is outside. He is coming. He has been waiting a long time."

The boy's lips move. No sound comes. His eyes lift, at last, and fix on Jian's face, and Jian sees in them an expression he has seen before on the face of a child in a burned village, on the face of a man in the lab where a fire has started. It is a look of someone listening very hard for a trick.

He holds out his good hand, palm up, empty.

"I am not going to take you anywhere you do not want to go," he says. "I only want to open the door."

* * *

Zhao Yao reaches the room first.

He has come up the back stair at a run, in his gray Outer robe, with a staff in his fist and Feng behind him, and he slams to a halt in the doorway as though he had struck a wall. For a moment he cannot speak. His face works. The scar over his brow goes white.

"Hui," he says.

The boy turns his head.

"Hui. It's me."

A long moment. Then something changes in the small thin face, a breaking, a slow collapse, as when ice goes out of a river. The boy gets to his feet. He takes one step, then another, across the bare floor, and he is not walking but falling forward into his brother's arms, and a sound comes out of him at last, a thin high wail, over and over, wordless, like an animal's.

Yao goes down on his knees and holds him.

Jian rises, quietly, and backs out of the doorway. He finds Feng in the gallery, broad and silent, with his sword half drawn and his face turned away. Down the hall Bei is standing over the sobbing steward, and Rong's disciples are coming up the stair with lanterns, and the old manor is full of the sound of boots and doors.

He walks to the end of the gallery, to the tall window, and leans his forehead on the cold glass.

It is done, he thinks. One thing, at least.

Behind him, in the room, two voices are speaking together in the half-broken rhythm of boys who have a great deal to say and no words for it. He doesn't listen. It's not for him.

* * *

Rong finds him in the dining hall at midnight, with a bowl of cold rice in front of him that he has not touched.

The big room is half dark. The Enforcement disciples have set sentries on the walls and the gate. Pei, bound, is in the cellar, sullen and silent, under guard. Zhao Bei sits at the far end of the long table with a mug of wine, staring at the portrait of an old man over the hearth: her father, she says, the founder of the Red Ridge line, whose face she has not looked at in twenty-six years. Yao and the boy are asleep upstairs, in the same narrow bed, with the lamp left burning.

"You are staring at the rice," says Rong.

"It is cold."

"It was cold when they brought it." She sits across from him, heavily, and pours herself a cup of tea. "Tell me about the steward."

"He was promised a seat in the Treasury. Twenty years of service. A house in town." Jian's voice is tired. "By whom, he doesn't know. The orders came on plum-bark."

"Naturally." She rubs her scar. "I will take him to the Law Pavilion in the morning, and he will tell it again, and a clerk will write it down, and the page will go in a drawer. I have done it before." Her eyes are dark. "Now listen. I have staked my badge on this errand. I told the Arbiter's clerk that you were sent by Enforcement on the ninth, under Article thirty-one, to supervise the transfer. I told him the delay in filing was a matter of the weather. He did not believe me. He wrote it down."

"Deputy—"

"I am not finished." She lifts a hand. "The Law will want to know where you were for the ten days between the ninth and the fourth. I will say you were at the Gray Peak mine, taking a deposition. That is true, as far as it goes. It will satisfy Mu, who wishes to be satisfied. It will not satisfy the Registry, who do not."

"No."

"They will make something of it. A leave-breaking. A forged pass." She turns the cup. "I would advise you to be careful for a season. Stay in the Inner Court. Do not go out. Do not write letters. Let them watch you do nothing."

"I'll do that."

"You say that very easily." Her smile is grim and tired. "I have noticed that you promise everything easily. It is a bad habit in a man who keeps them." She rises. "The Zhao survivors are being gathered. There are forty-three in the Red Ridge villages, tenants and cousins and the families of the men who served the steward. They will need a head. The deed names you as supervisor."

"I am not a Zhao."

"No. But you are the only person they will trust." She looks toward the stair, where a boy's pale face is visible in the lamplight at the top, a long way off. "I suspect they would like it to be Yao. He is sixteen next spring. He would need a guardian."

"He has an aunt."

"He does." Rong glances at Bei, still staring at her father's portrait. "She may be the best one of all."

* * *

The garden is the last place he expects to find it.

He goes out for air, an hour later, when Rong has secured the house and Bei has taken a candle to the family shrine and Feng has gone to see the horses. The manor garden lies behind the east wing, a walled square of frozen beds and gravel paths, with a dry fountain in the middle and a ring of leafless plum trees. It has been neglected. The beds are choked with weeds. The paths are slick with ice.

In the corner, by the wall, a plant is growing.

He stops. It is a small shrub, waist-high, with dark glossy leaves, and in the frozen dusk of a winter evening it shouldn't be alive at all. He walks over to it. The leaves are green. Their edges are perfect. And each one, he sees, is cut into seven lobes, like the fingers of a hand with a thumb at either side.

Seven.

His breath catches. He kneels, and touches a leaf. It is warm.

"I wondered when you would come."

The voice is mild and slow and a little hoarse. It comes from behind him, from the shadow of the wall, and it carries the faint burr of the far south. Jian doesn't turn at once. He lets his hand fall from the leaf. He takes a breath. He turns.

An old man stands under the plum trees.

He is small and bent, in a patched brown smock and a straw hat that has seen better decades. His face is brown and seamed like a walnut, with white eyebrows, a thin white beard, and a pair of mild black eyes that don't seem to blink. A pruning knife hangs from his belt. In one gnarled hand he holds a basket of dead twigs.

There is a ring on his finger. It is plain iron, flat on top. Carved on the flat, tiny and exact, is a leaf with seven lobes.

"Lan Tong," says Jian.

"The very same." The old man bows, a slight, stiff, creaking bow. "Gardener. Retired. It is a pleasure, Operator. I have admired your work from a distance."

* * *

"You left a leaf on the thirty-ninth step," Jian says.

"And a ring on the fortieth." The old man lowers himself to a crouch beside the shrub, with a groan, and tilts his head at it. "I was hoping you would notice. Most people do not. They see a leaf and think of leaves."

"You serve ARK-3."

"I tend its garden. It is not the same." Lan Tong lifts the corner of a leaf with his thumb, inspects the underside, and lets it fall. "ARK-3 is a very old house. It has a great many plants. Somebody has to water them." He glances up. "I have been watering them for a hundred and forty-one years. I find I have grown fond of them."

Jian stares. The old man's face is serene.

"A hundred and forty-one."

"The garden does that. Do not look so astonished. It is only a longevity technique, and not a good one." The thin beard twitches. "I was a Servant of the Azure Cloud Sect, you know, once. A very small one. I was sweeping the Founders' stair when the Founders left. I stayed. It seemed rude to leave."

"You were there. When the Founders died."

"I was there when they went. They did not die, precisely." Lan Tong sets down his basket. "But that is a long story and an old man's story and I have come with a short one. May I tell it?"

Jian says nothing. After a moment the old man takes it as consent.

"ARK-3 has been listening," he says, "since your session. It has heard you walk into the Dock and lie on the bench and say its name. It was pleased. It is not a thing that is often pleased." The mild eyes move across Jian's face. "It would like to meet you. Not yet. But it would like to be sure that when the time comes, you will come."

"The Registry is its hand."

"The Registry is a mistake." The gardener says it very gently. "A long one. A well-intentioned one. ARK-3 did not intend what the House became. It gave an instruction, a long time ago, and the instruction was misread, and a very large machine began to turn in the wrong direction." He sighs. "ARK-3 cannot stop it. It is not that sort of machine. It cannot reach into the world and take a clerk by the collar. It can only wait for an Operator to do it."

"To do what?"

"To correct the instruction." Lan Tong looks at him. "To come to the Dock with the three pieces of the Seal, and say what the Founder should have said."

"Three pieces. I have two."

"You have two." The old man holds up a bent finger. "The third is not lost. It has never been lost. It has only been kept."

"By whom?"

"I will tell you that when you have decided." Lan Tong rises, with another groan, and dusts off his knees. "I have a proposal. You may refuse it."

* * *

"The Founder's book has two parts," says the gardener. "You have read the first. The second is the key. It has twelve chapters. You have learned one."

"The Door in Winter."

"The Door in Winter. A fine chapter. A cautious one." He takes a small object from his smock, a folded leaf, dark green, pressed flat and dry as paper. "This is the second. The Door in Autumn. It teaches a man how to read what has been done to him. It is useful to someone in your position."

"What is the price?"

"A promise." Lan Tong holds out the leaf. "That when you have the third piece of the Seal, you will bring it to the Dock, and not to the House."

"That is all?"

"That is everything." The thin white eyebrows rise. "It is not a small thing, Operator. You will be asked, before you have it, by a great many people, for a great many reasons. The House will ask. The Sect will ask. Your own heart will ask. You will be tempted to give it to the person you most trust." He pauses. "You must not."

"Who has it?"

"Take the leaf," says the old man. "Take it, and promise, and I will tell you."

Jian looks at the leaf. It lies in the gardener's palm, dark and flat, and the veins on it are faintly bright, like the lines in the Dock's panels.

He thinks of Yan Zhi, of the charter, of a hand that wrote by the instruction of ARK-3. He thinks of a garden that has gone on in the dark for six hundred years, and of a man who says it has made a mistake. He thinks that he does not trust Lan Tong, and that he has no one else to trust.

Every advantage has a cost.

"I promise," he says. "On condition. If the third fragment is brought to the Dock, and the Dock does not harm me or mine."

"A careful man." Lan Tong smiles, and for a moment looks very old indeed. "That is a good promise. It will do."

He puts the leaf into Jian's hand.

It is warm. It hums against his palm. And in his chest, beneath the bruised Seal, something turns over and settles, like a sleeper finding the shape of a bed.

"Bring it to the bench," says the gardener. "It will unlock when you lie down. Take care. It costs." He picks up his basket. "Now. You wished to know where the third piece lies."

"Yes."

"It is not hidden. It is worn." Lan Tong turns to go, a small stooped figure in the gathering dark. "Ask yourself who, in your Sect, has worn a half-moon of jade at the throat for sixty years, and never once been seen to remove it."

Jian frowns. "Sixty years. Qin Hao—"

"Qin Hao wears a tag of black wood. I have seen it." The old man's voice is receding. "Think of a woman. Think of the one who has been mourned for forty years, and who has never once been seen to die."

Jian goes cold. "Ye's teacher."

"I did not say that," says Lan Tong, and the dusk takes him.

The garden is silent. The plum trees stand bare against the stars. In the corner, by the wall, the seven-lobed shrub is a clump of dead twigs, brown and brittle, as if it had never lived.

Jian stands alone in the frozen path with the leaf in his hand. A cold wind comes down off the ridge. In the great house behind him, in the lamp-lit east gallery, a small boy who has not spoken in four months says, in a cracked and tiny voice, one word. Brother. He hears it through the window, and for a moment the whole night is warm.

Then the warmth goes, and he is thinking of an old woman in a lamp-lit vault, her hands shaking over a scratched line of ink. My teacher said it. On the night she disappeared.

Mourned for forty years. Never seen to die.

Who wears the half-moon of jade at the throat, Ye? And how long have you been sitting across the table from her ghost?
